# Use AI This Election

### ...

I’m not saying AI is superintelligent or can decide better than you can. I’m saying that if you - like me - spend an hour or so doing research before voting on local seats, AI can aid that research very effectively. And if you don’t do that research - because you weren’t willing to waste an hour on it before - AI makes it so much faster that you might want to start.

I gave Claude a prompt something like (edited for coherence):

> I’ll be voting in the June 2026 California primary. I’m a centrist liberal abundance YIMBY whose favorite political writers are Kelsey Piper, Matt Yglesias, and Ezra Klein. I’m wary of government overreach, but I’m not a doctrinaire libertarian and want to help people when we can figure ways to do it that work. I’m going to ask you about each race on my ballot, and I’d like for you to list the various candidates’ bios, policies, endorsements, your read on the most important differences between them, and your advice for me as I try to make my choice.

…and got back answers like the following:

The most important differences, and my read for the Piper view The structured literacy litmus test points hard to Muratsuchi. He is the only candidate in this field who has actually moved policy on the thing Piper considers most urgent. His official candidate statement explicitly cites “phonics-based reading instruction based on the science of reading” as something he coauthored and delivered funding for. That is, almost verbatim, the policy Piper has spent the last year writing about. Nobody else in the field has a comparable record on this issue. Rendon is the second-strongest plausible fit, but with caveats. Twenty years running an early-childhood program is genuinely relevant experience, and TK (transitional kindergarten) expansion is one of the more evidence-supported things California has done in K–12. But his charter-accountability work as Speaker generally meant more regulation on charters, which cuts against the Piper-flavored openness to alternative models. He’s a competent establishment Democrat; he’d be a fine superintendent, just not specifically the structured-literacy crusader. Barrera is the candidate Piper would be most skeptical of. Not because he’s a bad person — he’s a long-serving school board president, presumably competent — but because the CTA endorsement is his political identity in this race, and Piper’s whole thesis is that CTA-aligned politics has been one of the structural reasons California can’t adopt the reforms that worked elsewhere. Barrera’s stated priorities (more funding, easier teacher pathways) are CTA priorities, not reform priorities. If you’re voting the Piper view, this is the one to skip. Henderson and Lara are further from the Piper view. Henderson’s “standardized testing reform” plus the pension-divestment-from-the-war-machine framing reads as movement-left rather than evidence-driven; Piper has been pointedly critical of detracking and of treating testing as the enemy. Lara is more or less explicitly the union-left candidate. Mattammal is the awkward case. He is the candidate closest to Piper on school choice and microschools specifically — that’s basically her own model. But he’s running with essentially no political coalition or governing experience, and the Piper view, while choice-friendly, is not “burn down public schools” — it’s “fix the actual reading instruction in the schools that most kids will continue to attend.” A statewide superintendent who can’t move CTA-dominated Sacramento isn’t useful for that goal. Mattammal also doesn’t appear to have an articulated policy program on structured literacy or accountability, just on alternatives. Probably not the right fit even on a choice-sympathetic reading. Shaw is obviously off the table on the Piper view. Piper is a Bay Area liberal who supports trans kids and has no interest in culture-war education politics. The Moms for Liberty endorsement is disqualifying on its own. Newman is the dark horse. Co-authored Prop. 2 with Muratsuchi, chaired Senate Education, military background, now an academic fellow rather than a Sacramento insider. He hasn’t been as visibly identified with structured literacy as Muratsuchi has, but he’s broadly in the same evidence-and-accountability lane. The Building Trades endorsement is unusual — it suggests he’s running a coalition strategy aimed at facilities/jobs rather than CTA — and that might actually be a positive signal for someone trying to operate independently of the dominant teachers’ union politics. Bottom line For the Piper view, Muratsuchi is the clearest fit in the field. He’s the only candidate who has actually legislated structured literacy funding, he has the directly relevant policy chops (former Education Committee chair, Prop. 2), and his endorsement coalition (CFT, administrators, classified employees) is just slightly off-axis from the dominant CTA-controlled lane in a way that suggests some independence. He’s also reasonably likely to make the November runoff, which matters: a vote for the second-best candidate who finishes fourth doesn’t accomplish anything. If you wanted to express a sharper “I want a real outsider reformer” view rather than working within the field as it exists, Mattammal is the only option, but at significant cost in viability and breadth of program. For “I just want a competent Democrat who’ll be fine,” Rendon and Newman are both reasonable. But for “I want the candidate most likely to actually push the structured-literacy / accountability agenda Piper writes about,” it’s Muratsuchi.
